name: Urine therapy

lead: Urine therapy, also called urotherapy or shivambu, means drinking one's own urine or applying it to the skin or gums for health or cosmetic purposes, with the aim of clearer, younger-looking skin. It has roots in several cultures, including medieval hatha yoga, and was popularised in modern times by the British naturopath John W. Armstrong.

Proponents attribute effects to substances in urine, such as urea or claimed stem cells. Urine is over 95 percent water, and commercial urea creams use synthetic urea at far higher concentrations than urine provides. A reference source states there is no scientific evidence of therapeutic benefit from untreated urine.

paras: Followers drink their own urine, sometimes aged, or massage it into skin or gums, typically as a daily morning routine. Some apply it as a facial toner.

Medical sources report no demonstrated benefit and note microbial contamination concerns. The American Cancer Society states that evidence does not support urine or urea helping cancer patients. One looksmax.org user posted a report of a negative experience drinking aged urine, describing a burning throat and nausea.

web.title: Microbial evaluation of urine as alternative therapy

angle.text: Followers drink or apply urine, sometimes aged, hoping for skin renewal and a younger, clearer look. The practice has roots in yoga traditions, and medical sources report no demonstrated therapeutic benefit from untreated urine.

lead: Urine therapy, also called urotherapy, urinotherapy, shivambu or auto-urine therapy, is an alternative-medicine practice in which a person uses their own urine for medicinal or cosmetic purposes, including drinking it and massaging it into the skin or gums. In medieval hatha yoga a related practice was called amaroli [1].

In appearance terms, practitioners use it as a rejuvenation method. The chain they describe runs from urine applied to or drunk by the person, to components proponents credit with healing or renewing action (urea, hormones, enzymes and, in some forum accounts, 'stem cells'), to a clearer, fresher-looking complexion [1][2]. Within looksmaxxing forums the emphasis is on facial rejuvenation, with some proponents favouring aged or fermented urine [2].

Medical and reference sources report that no scientific evidence supports therapeutic use of untreated urine [1]. Urine is more than 95 percent water, with urea, chloride, sodium, potassium and creatinine as main solutes, according to a 1971 NASA report summarised on Wikipedia [1]. Purified urea, by contrast, is an established dermatology ingredient used in creams at concentrations far above what urine provides [1][3].

The word urotherapy is also used in paediatric urology for non-surgical bladder training and behavioural treatment of bladder and bowel dysfunction; that usage is unrelated to the practice described here [4].

paras: Urine appears in several traditional remedy systems and older medical texts, including Solomon's English Physician (1665) and A Dictionary of Practical Materia Medica (1902). Roman dentists reportedly used it to whiten teeth, an early Islamic jurist permitted camel urine for medicinal purposes, and traditional remedies in Mexico and Nigeria have used urine [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that medieval European physicians used urine mainly for diagnosis (uroscopy) while folk remedies kept topical uses, and that texts such as the Damar Tantra are said to describe drinking urine as shivambu, though it states the dating of such traditions is not verified [5].

subs.h: John W. Armstrong and The Water of Life
paras: The British naturopath John W. Armstrong popularised drinking one's own urine in the early 20th century. He was influenced by his family's use of urine for stings and toothaches, by a loose reading of Proverbs 5:15 and by a 45-day fast on urine and tap water that he credited for his own recovery. He reportedly began prescribing urine regimens in 1918, treated thousands of patients, and published The Water of Life: A Treatise on Urine Therapy in 1944, which became a founding text of the field [1]. Brief 1940s items titled Urine therapy appeared in the medical journals Experientia and The Medical Press [6][7].

Armstrong's book inspired the Gujarati work Manav Mootra (1959) by the Gandhian reformer Raojibhai Manibhai Patel. Later books often cite a text called Shivambu Kalpa, which Wikipedia describes as not well attested. The medical anthropologist Joseph Alter has argued that modern Indian practice resembles Armstrong's version more than traditional Ayurveda or yoga, whose classical texts mention urine only in passing [1]. Morarji Desai, who was India's Prime Minister from 1977 to 1979, was a long-time practitioner who spoke about drinking urine on CBS's 60 Minutes in 1978 and attributed his longevity to it; he died in 1995 at age 99 [8]. A Chinese Urine Therapy Association claiming thousands of members was listed as an illegal organisation by the Ministry of Civil Affairs in 2016 [1].

Grokipedia reports that Martha Christy's Your Own Perfect Medicine (1996) claimed urine contains hundreds of beneficial substances, that the NFL player Ben Jones said in 2015 he had used it for performance, and that the Indian actor Paresh Rawal said in April 2025 that he drank his own urine daily for a knee injury [5]. These accounts are reported by an AI-generated source and are listed here as attributed claims only. Wikipedia records a January 2022 social-media claim that urine therapy could counter COVID-19, which Reuters fact-checked [1].

Practitioners describe two broad routes: drinking urine (urophagia) and applying it to skin or gums.[1] Looksmaxxing guides present it mainly as a facial rejuvenation method rather than a general health regimen.[2] Details of preparation vary between sources and are not reproduced here.

Proponents claim benefits for a wide range of conditions and for general health. Some practitioners claim anti-cancer effects, and some cancer clinics in Mexico have offered urotherapy alongside other alternative treatments.[1] A January 2022 social-media claim that urine therapy could cure COVID-19 was fact-checked by Reuters.[1]

Within looksmaxxing forums, a user guide describes urine therapy as a rejuvenation method, citing the idea that urine contains stem cells and other properties that proponents say rejuvenate the face, and that fermenting or ageing urine increases them.[2]

Proponents' topical uses include applying urine to acne, eczema, psoriasis and the scalp, or using it as an overnight face mask [5]. Looksmaxxing posts present it as a facial rejuvenation method, citing claimed stem cells and other components [2]. Dermatology's own use of urea is separate: urea-containing creams rehydrate skin, and preparations of up to 40 percent are used for psoriasis, xerosis, ichthyosis, eczema, keratosis and calluses [3]. Wikipedia states that actual urine is too dilute to act like those creams [1].

sections.h: Composition of urine and relation to urea creams
paras: A 1971 NASA report found urine to be more than 95 percent water, with urea (about 9.3 g/L), chloride, sodium, potassium and creatinine as main solutes.[1] Urea is the main nitrogen-containing compound in mammalian urine; the liver makes it through the urea cycle and the kidneys excrete it, and over time it breaks down to ammonia, which is why stale urine smells stronger.[3]

Urea is also used in dermatology. Urea-containing creams rehydrate skin, and preparations of up to 40 percent are used for conditions such as psoriasis, eczema, ichthyosis, xerosis, keratosis and calluses.[3] Wikipedia's urine therapy article notes that synthetic urea creams work as a humectant and keratolytic at high concentrations, while actual urine is too dilute for that purpose.[1] Friedrich Wohler's 1828 synthesis of urea, which helped undermine vitalism, is a landmark in organic chemistry.[3]

No studies found testing urine therapy for skin, appearance or rejuvenation. Research on urotherapy in paediatric urology concerns bladder and bowel training and is unrelated to drinking or applying urine.[4]

Reference material states there is no scientific evidence of therapeutic use of untreated urine. The American Cancer Society said in 2008 that available evidence does not support urine or urea helping cancer patients [1]. The belief that urine relieves jellyfish stings is described as incorrect, with urination possibly worsening pain by triggering remaining stinging cells [1]. Skeptical writers including Martin Gardner and Robert Todd Carroll have criticised the practice [1].

A 2010 microbiology study in the Pan African Medical Journal by Ogunshe and colleagues cultured 116 bacterial isolates from the urine of healthy children aged 5 to 11 and from cow urine, including E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, Shigella and Salmonella, and reported many isolates resistant to multiple antibiotics; the authors state there is no documented scientific or clinical evidence of benefit and argue home use could delay appropriate care. The study did not test whether drinking urine causes illness, and the authors' conclusions are inferences from culture data [1][9].

Grokipedia lists reported harms including dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, a 2022 case report of severe hypernatremia (sodium above 190 mmol/L) with neurological symptoms in a person who drank urine, and eye injuries after urine was applied to the eyes [5]. It also notes that applying whole urine to skin for long periods has been described as potentially damaging the skin barrier, in contrast to purified urea [5]. Cameroon's health ministry is reported there to have warned against drinking urine in 2020 [5].

Urine-related practices appear in several regions. A Chinese Urine Therapy Association claiming thousands of members was listed as illegal by the Ministry of Civil Affairs in 2016. In 2022 a self-described holy man in Thailand was arrested after followers were seen consuming his bodily waste. Bottled camel urine is sold in the Arabian Peninsula as prophetic medicine, and in 2015 Saudi police arrested a man for selling his own urine as camel urine.[1]

In the Arabian Peninsula, camel urine is sold as prophetic medicine. Wikipedia also records a Zhejiang dish, virgin boy eggs, boiled in boys' urine, and a 2003 BBC report on a Thai doctor promoting urine therapy that the Department of Thai Traditional Medicine said it had no record of [1].

A looksmax.org thread presents urine therapy as a rejuvenation practice, including the claim that fermenting or ageing urine increases stem cells. In the same thread the author reported a negative experience with drinking aged urine while sunbathing, describing a burning throat and nausea, and advised others against drinking aged urine.[2] Another user replied that the practice seemed excessive.[2]

lore.intro: Urine therapy is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a fringe rejuvenation practice, with proponents' guides and at least one user warning from experience.[2]
